title: Week 10: Vulnerability Assessment & Penetration Testing (VAPT) & Nessus Lab
subject: Information Assurance and Security
description: VA vs. PT comparison, CVSS v3.1/v4.0 metrics and severity ratings, PTES penetration testing lifecycle, enterprise vulnerability remediation, and Tenable Nessus Essentials lab.
sourceFile: BCS411L S2W10 Vulnerability Assessment & Penetration Testing (VAPT).pdf, BCS411L S2W10 Lab Vulnerability Assessment.pdf

questions.question: Why is inspecting configuration files or architecture diagrams alone insufficient to evaluate an organization's true security posture?
options: Defensive controls suffer from configuration drift, unpatched dependencies, custom code logic flaws, and unintended operational interactions
Architecture diagrams are always encrypted with AES-256
Firewalls automatically disable all logging after 24 hours
Configuration files cannot be read on Linux or Windows hosts
questions.answer: Defensive controls suffer from configuration drift, unpatched dependencies, custom code logic flaws, and unintended operational interactions
questions.explanation: VAPT is needed because live environments diverge from static diagrams due to configuration drift, unpatched software, logical flaws, and runtime interactions.

questions.question: Which statement accurately contrasts Vulnerability Assessment (VA) and Penetration Testing (PT)?
options: VA is breadth-oriented, primarily automated, and catalogs potential flaws without exploitation; PT is depth-oriented, manual/goal-driven, and actively exploits and chains flaws
VA actively exploits systems to steal data; PT only runs automated port scans
VA has an extremely low false positive rate; PT has a high false positive rate
VA is conducted once a decade; PT is run automatically every five minutes
questions.answer: VA is breadth-oriented, primarily automated, and catalogs potential flaws without exploitation; PT is depth-oriented, manual/goal-driven, and actively exploits and chains flaws
questions.explanation: VA focuses on breadth (cataloging all known flaws with automated tools like Nessus/Qualys/OpenVAS), whereas PT focuses on depth (validating real-world exploitability and business impact).

questions.question: What is the primary deliverable of a Penetration Test compared to a Vulnerability Assessment?
options: PT delivers Proof-of-Concept (PoC) exploit paths and impact reports; VA delivers a prioritized list of unpatched assets and potential flaws
PT delivers raw Nmap XML files only; VA delivers signed legal contracts
PT delivers hardware write-blockers; VA delivers SIEM correlation rules
Both deliver identical unvalidated scanner spreadsheets
questions.answer: PT delivers Proof-of-Concept (PoC) exploit paths and impact reports; VA delivers a prioritized list of unpatched assets and potential flaws
questions.explanation: VA outputs a prioritized inventory of unpatched flaws (requiring triage for false positives), while PT proves exploitability with PoC attack paths and business impact.

questions.question: How does 'Vulnerability Chaining' demonstrate the limitation of relying purely on automated Vulnerability Assessment scanners?
options: Automated scanners rate minor flaws in isolation, missing how a human tester can combine them (e.g., an IDOR plus a weak password policy) to achieve full system compromise
Automated scanners can only scan one IP address per year
Vulnerability chaining prevents Nessus from reading open ports
Automated scanners automatically patch vulnerabilities before reporting them
questions.answer: Automated scanners rate minor flaws in isolation, missing how a human tester can combine them (e.g., an IDOR plus a weak password policy) to achieve full system compromise
questions.explanation: A scanner may mark two flaws as Low or Medium individually, whereas a penetration tester chains them together to bypass controls, escalate privileges, and pivot.

questions.question: In the CVSS vector string `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`, what does `AV:N/PR:N/UI:N` indicate?
options: The vulnerability is exploitable over the Network, requires No Privileges, and requires No User Interaction
The vulnerability requires Physical access, High privileges, and User Interaction
The vulnerability is Local only, requires Low privileges, and has No Availability impact
The vulnerability is Adjacent-network only and changes the Hypervisor scope
questions.answer: The vulnerability is exploitable over the Network, requires No Privileges, and requires No User Interaction
questions.explanation: AV:N = Attack Vector: Network, PR:N = Privileges Required: None, UI:N = User Interaction: None — the classic signature of an unauthenticated remotely exploitable flaw.

questions.question: Which CVSS metric group measures characteristics that change over time, such as Exploit Code Maturity, Remediation Level, and Report Confidence?
options: Temporal Metric Group
Base Metric Group
Environmental Metric Group
Perimeter Metric Group
questions.answer: Temporal Metric Group
questions.explanation: Base metrics capture intrinsic constant traits; Temporal metrics track evolving traits (exploit maturity, patches, confidence); Environmental metrics tailor scores to an organization's infrastructure and compensating controls.

questions.question: In CVSS v3.1, when is the Scope (`S`) metric rated as Changed (`S:C`) instead of Unchanged (`S:U`)?
options: When a vulnerability in one component allows an attacker to impact resources beyond its security authority, such as a VM flaw compromising the underlying Host Hypervisor
When the vulnerability only affects a single unauthenticated user's browser cookie
When an organization moves a server from on-premises to the cloud
When the CVSS base score is exactly 0.0
questions.answer: When a vulnerability in one component allows an attacker to impact resources beyond its security authority, such as a VM flaw compromising the underlying Host Hypervisor
questions.explanation: Scope is Changed (`S:C`) when exploitation crosses a security authorization boundary, such as escaping a guest Virtual Machine to compromise the host hypervisor.

questions.question: According to the CVSS v3.1 / v4.0 severity table, which score range corresponds to 'Critical' and what is its typical operational remediation urgency?
options: 9.0 – 10.0; Emergency Response (e.g., 24–72 hours)
7.0 – 8.9; Scheduled patch windows (e.g., 30–60 days)
4.0 – 6.9; Priority remediation (e.g., 7–14 days)
0.1 – 3.9; Emergency Response (within 1 hour)
questions.answer: 9.0 – 10.0; Emergency Response (e.g., 24–72 hours)
questions.explanation: CVSS ratings: 0.0 None, 0.1–3.9 Low (standard maintenance), 4.0–6.9 Medium (30–60 days), 7.0–8.9 High (7–14 days), and 9.0–10.0 Critical (Emergency Response, 24–72 hours).

questions.question: What qualitative severity rating and remediation window apply to a vulnerability with a CVSS Base Score of 7.8?
options: High; priority remediation required (e.g., 7–14 days)
Medium; remediate within 30–60 days
Critical; emergency response in 24–72 hours
Low; remediate during standard maintenance cycles
questions.answer: High; priority remediation required (e.g., 7–14 days)
questions.explanation: Scores from 7.0 to 8.9 are rated High and typically require priority remediation within 7–14 days.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the six phases in the Penetration Testing Execution Standard (PTES) lifecycle?
options: 1. Pre-Engagement -> 2. Reconnaissance -> 3. Threat Modeling / Vulnerability Analysis -> 4. Exploitation -> 5. Post-Exploitation -> 6. Reporting
1. Exploitation -> 2. Pre-Engagement -> 3. Reconnaissance -> 4. Reporting -> 5. Threat Modeling -> 6. Post-Exploitation
1. Reconnaissance -> 2. Pre-Engagement -> 3. Reporting -> 4. Exploitation -> 5. Vulnerability Analysis -> 6. Post-Exploitation
1. Asset Discovery -> 2. Validation Scanning -> 3. Pre-Engagement -> 4. Patching -> 5. Exploitation -> 6. Archiving
questions.answer: 1. Pre-Engagement -> 2. Reconnaissance -> 3. Threat Modeling / Vulnerability Analysis -> 4. Exploitation -> 5. Post-Exploitation -> 6. Reporting
questions.explanation: PTES (alongside NIST SP 800-115) progresses from legal Pre-Engagement scoping to Reconnaissance, Threat Modeling/Vulnerability Analysis, Exploitation, Post-Exploitation/Pivoting, and Reporting.

questions.question: Before running any technical command in a penetration test, what three legal and operational artifacts must be established during Pre-Engagement?
options: Rules of Engagement (RoE), Scope Definition (In-Scope vs. Out-of-Scope), and signed Authorization / Permission to Test ('Get Out of Jail Free' letter)
SIEM correlation rules, WORM storage, and SHA-256 hashes
Executive Summary, PoC exploit code, and validation re-scans
Nessus activation key, Kali ISO checksum, and Metasploitable2 snapshot
questions.answer: Rules of Engagement (RoE), Scope Definition (In-Scope vs. Out-of-Scope), and signed Authorization / Permission to Test ('Get Out of Jail Free' letter)
questions.explanation: Pre-Engagement defines explicit IP/domain targets, prohibited techniques (e.g., DoS, social engineering), testing windows, emergency contacts, and signed authorization protecting testers from legal liability.

questions.question: During PTES Phase 5 (Post-Exploitation & Pivoting), what does 'Pivoting / Lateral Movement' refer to?
options: Using an already compromised host as a network jump-box to bypass internal firewalls and reach isolated internal subnets
Writing an executive summary slide deck for the Board of Directors
Running an unauthenticated Nessus Basic Network Scan from outside the perimeter
Enabling Block Public Access on an Amazon S3 bucket
questions.answer: Using an already compromised host as a network jump-box to bypass internal firewalls and reach isolated internal subnets
questions.explanation: Post-exploitation includes Local Privilege Escalation (LPE to root/SYSTEM), Pivoting/Lateral Movement via a compromised jump-box, and Persistence demonstration.

questions.question: If a penetration tester discovers a critical Zero-Day vulnerability on a system explicitly marked Out-of-Scope during an active engagement, what should they do?
options: Stop any interaction with the out-of-scope system immediately, document the observation safely, and notify the client's emergency contact per the Rules of Engagement
Exploit the Zero-Day immediately to prove maximum business impact
Upload the target's proprietary firmware to VirusTotal
Ignore it completely and delete all testing notes
questions.answer: Stop any interaction with the out-of-scope system immediately, document the observation safely, and notify the client's emergency contact per the Rules of Engagement
questions.explanation: Testing or exploiting Out-of-Scope targets violates written authorization and creates civil/criminal liability; testers must cease interaction and escalate through the RoE emergency contact.

questions.question: What are the four continuous stages of the Enterprise Vulnerability Remediation Lifecycle?
options: 1. Asset Discovery -> 2. Assessment & Scanning -> 3. Prioritization & Risk -> 4. Remediation / Patching -> Verification Scan
1. Exploitation -> 2. Ransom Demand -> 3. Exfiltration -> 4. Cleanup
1. Preparation -> 2. Memory Dumping -> 3. Chain of Custody -> 4. Litigation
1. Disassembly -> 2. Debugging -> 3. YARA Authoring -> 4. Sandbox Reset
questions.answer: 1. Asset Discovery -> 2. Assessment & Scanning -> 3. Prioritization & Risk -> 4. Remediation / Patching -> Verification Scan
questions.explanation: Enterprise vulnerability management cycles continuously through Continuous Asset Discovery, Assessment & Scanning, Contextual Risk Prioritization, Remediation/Mitigation, and Validation Scanning.

questions.question: Why might a vulnerability with a High CVSS Base Score (e.g., 8.5) be assigned a LOW operational remediation priority inside an enterprise program?
options: If the affected asset is air-gapped, non-critical, has no known active exploit, or is protected by strong compensating controls (like a WAF or VLAN isolation)
Because CVSS scores above 7.0 are ignored by compliance frameworks
Because Nessus marks all High vulnerabilities as Informational (Blue)
Because High CVSS vulnerabilities cannot be patched
questions.answer: If the affected asset is air-gapped, non-critical, has no known active exploit, or is protected by strong compensating controls (like a WAF or VLAN isolation)
questions.explanation: Contextual Risk Prioritization combines CVSS Base Scores with threat context (active exploit availability) and business criticality/exposure (public-facing vs. air-gapped).

questions.question: If a Critical vulnerability (CVSS 9.8) affects a legacy application that cannot be patched without breaking business operations, what is the best response?
options: Implement compensating controls (mitigation) such as deploying a WAF virtual patch rule, isolating the legacy host behind a restricted VLAN, and tightening access controls
Disable all logging on the legacy server so scanners stop alerting
Expose the server directly to the public internet to distribute load
Manually lower the CVSS score to 0.0 in the PDF report
questions.answer: Implement compensating controls (mitigation) such as deploying a WAF virtual patch rule, isolating the legacy host behind a restricted VLAN, and tightening access controls
questions.explanation: When root remediation (patching) is technically impossible, organizations apply Mitigation / Compensating Controls such as WAF rules or VLAN network isolation.

questions.question: In the Week 10 Nessus Essentials lab, which TCP port hosts the Nessus Web Console UI, and which systemd service manages the Nessus daemon on Linux?
options: Port 8834 (`https://localhost:8834`); managed by `nessusd.service`
Port 8080 (`http://localhost:8080`); managed by `apache2.service`
Port 6514 (`https://localhost:6514`); managed by `syslog.service`
Port 443 (`https://localhost:443`); managed by `wazuh-agent.service`
questions.answer: Port 8834 (`https://localhost:8834`); managed by `nessusd.service`
questions.explanation: After installing the `.deb` package, you start and enable `nessusd.service` and access the Nessus Web UI at `https://localhost:8834` (or `https://127.0.0.1:8834`).

questions.question: When configuring the `Victim_VM_Vulnerability_Assessment` scan using the Basic Network Scan template in the lab, which Discovery and Assessment settings are selected?
options: Discovery: `Port scan (all ports)`; Assessment: `Scan for known vulnerabilities (default)`
Discovery: `Ping only (no ports)`; Assessment: `Brute force all passwords`
Discovery: `Top 10 ports`; Assessment: `Exploit and delete database`
Discovery: `Disabled`; Assessment: `Compliance audit only`
questions.answer: Discovery: `Port scan (all ports)`; Assessment: `Scan for known vulnerabilities (default)`
questions.explanation: Step 2.2 specifies Targets `192.168.56.20`, Discovery Scan Type `Port scan (all ports)`, and Assessment Scan Type `Scan for known vulnerabilities (default)`.

questions.question: In Nessus Essentials, what color codes correspond to Critical, High, Medium, Low, and Info findings respectively?
options: Critical = Red, High = Orange, Medium = Yellow, Low = Green, Info = Blue
Critical = Black, High = Red, Medium = Purple, Low = Blue, Info = White
Critical = Blue, High = Green, Medium = Yellow, Low = Orange, Info = Red
Critical = Purple, High = Pink, Medium = Gray, Low = Cyan, Info = Green
questions.answer: Critical = Red, High = Orange, Medium = Yellow, Low = Green, Info = Blue
questions.explanation: Nessus maps CVSS ranges to colors: Critical 9.0–10.0 (Red), High 7.0–8.9 (Orange), Medium 4.0–6.9 (Yellow), Low 0.1–3.9 (Green), and Info 0.0 (Blue).

questions.question: When inspecting a Critical finding (such as Bind Shell Backdoor Detection or vsftpd 2.3.4 Backdoor) in Nessus, which field contains the raw proof returned by the target host?
options: Plugin Output
Synopsis
Executive Summary
Folder Name
questions.answer: Plugin Output
questions.explanation: In Nessus plugin details: Synopsis summarizes the flaw, Description explains the root cause, Solution gives remediation steps, CVSS v3.1 Base Score shows the vector/score, and Plugin Output displays the raw proof from the target.

questions.question: What is the operational difference between exporting a Nessus 'Executive Summary' report versus a 'Custom / Detailed' technical report?
options: Executive Summary provides high-level distribution charts and strategic risk for leadership, whereas Detailed Technical Reports include full plugin outputs, affected ports, and step-by-step remediation for sysadmins
Executive Summary contains only raw PCAPs; Detailed Technical Reports contain only company logos
Executive Summary exploits vulnerabilities; Detailed Technical Reports uninstall Nessus
There is no difference; both export identical 1-page summaries
questions.answer: Executive Summary provides high-level distribution charts and strategic risk for leadership, whereas Detailed Technical Reports include full plugin outputs, affected ports, and step-by-step remediation for sysadmins
questions.explanation: Leadership uses the Executive Summary for high-level risk posture and compliance, while engineers and sysadmins need the Custom / Detailed Technical Report with plugin outputs and remediation instructions.

questions.topic: Nessus Lab: False Positives & Credentialed Scans
questions.question: Why might an automated unauthenticated Nessus scan report a 'False Positive,' and how does credentialed scanning mitigate it?
options: Unauthenticated scans rely on exposed service banners (which may show an older base version despite OS vendor backported security patches); credentialed scans log in to inspect exact installed package versions and patch levels
Unauthenticated scans never inspect banners; credentialed scans guess vulnerabilities based on hostname
Unauthenticated scans only check port 22; credentialed scans disable the firewall
Credentialed scans automatically fix false positives by deleting the service
questions.answer: Unauthenticated scans rely on exposed service banners (which may show an older base version despite OS vendor backported security patches); credentialed scans log in to inspect exact installed package versions and patch levels
questions.explanation: Distributions like Debian/RHEL backport security fixes without bumping the upstream version number in banners. Credentialed scanning authenticates via SSH/WinRM to verify actual package versions and registry keys.

questions.question: In the PTES lifecycle, which phase combines automated scan data with manual analysis to map assets and identify exploitable weaknesses before launching exploits?
options: Phase 3: Threat Modeling / Vulnerability Analysis
Phase 1: Pre-Engagement Interactions
Phase 5: Post-Exploitation & Pivoting
Phase 6: Reporting & Remediation Support
questions.answer: Phase 3: Threat Modeling / Vulnerability Analysis
questions.explanation: Following Reconnaissance (Phase 2), Threat Modeling / Vulnerability Analysis correlates automated and manual findings to identify exploitable paths before controlled Exploitation (Phase 4).

questions.question: Why does Penetration Testing carry a moderate risk of operational impact and require strict Rules of Engagement (RoE)?
options: Because testers actively execute exploit payloads and craft custom attack vectors that could crash services or corrupt data if uncontrolled
Because penetration testing requires physically unplugging every server rack
Because penetration testers never ask for permission before testing
Because penetration testing only inspects static PDF policy documents
questions.answer: Because testers actively execute exploit payloads and craft custom attack vectors that could crash services or corrupt data if uncontrolled
questions.explanation: Unlike non-intrusive VA scans, PT executes active exploits and tests SOC/Blue Team detection, requiring careful operational control and strict RoE boundaries.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the final stage ('Verification / Validation Scan') in the Vulnerability Remediation Lifecycle?
options: To re-scan patched assets and confirm the vulnerability has been resolved without introducing regressions
To perform initial asset discovery on unknown cloud accounts
To calculate the organization's annual cybersecurity insurance premium
To erase all scan history from the Nessus database
questions.answer: To re-scan patched assets and confirm the vulnerability has been resolved without introducing regressions
questions.explanation: Applying a patch or configuration change is only verified once a Validation Scan confirms the flaw is closed and no new issues were introduced.

questions.question: Which three core security properties are evaluated by the CVSS Impact Metrics (each rated None, Low, or High)?
options: Confidentiality (C), Integrity (I), and Availability (A)
Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting
Prevention, Detection, and Response
Attack Vector, Complexity, and Privileges
questions.answer: Confidentiality (C), Integrity (I), and Availability (A)
questions.explanation: CVSS Base Metrics split into Exploitability (AV, AC, PR, UI), Scope (S), and Impact (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability).

questions.question: Which four values are valid for the Attack Vector (AV) metric in CVSS v3.1?
options: Physical (P), Local (L), Adjacent (A), and Network (N)
Internal (I), External (E), Cloud (C), and Hybrid (H)
Passive (P), Active (A), Stealth (S), and Aggressive (G)
Low (L), Medium (M), High (H), and Critical (C)
questions.answer: Physical (P), Local (L), Adjacent (A), and Network (N)
questions.explanation: Attack Vector measures how far away an attacker can be to exploit the flaw: Physical (P), Local (L), Adjacent (A), or Network (N).

questions.question: During Nessus Essentials installation on Linux, what commands install the `.deb` package and verify that the daemon is running?
options: `sudo dpkg -i Nessus-10.*-ubuntu1110_amd64.deb` followed by `sudo systemctl start/enable/status nessusd.service`
`sudo apt install nmap -y` followed by `sudo nmap -sS localhost`
`sudo bash ./wazuh-install.sh -a` followed by `systemctl status wazuh-agent`
`pip install volatility3` followed by `vol -f mem.raw`
questions.answer: `sudo dpkg -i Nessus-10.*-ubuntu1110_amd64.deb` followed by `sudo systemctl start/enable/status nessusd.service`
questions.explanation: In Part 1 of the lab, students install the Nessus `.deb` via `dpkg -i`, start and enable `nessusd.service`, and verify status before opening `https://localhost:8834`.

questions.question: In the Sample Executive Summary Report Output from the Week 10 lab, what does the 'Info' category (CVSS 0.0, Blue) represent?
options: Contextual data detailing open ports, service banners, and host fingerprinting notes
Immediate remote code execution vulnerabilities without authentication
System crashes caused during active exploitation
Deprecated user passwords cracked during the scan
questions.answer: Contextual data detailing open ports, service banners, and host fingerprinting notes
questions.explanation: Info findings (CVSS 0.0, Blue) provide useful reconnaissance context such as open ports, service banners, and OS fingerprinting details rather than exploitable flaws.

questions.question: In PTES Post-Exploitation, what is the goal of Local Privilege Escalation (LPE) and Persistence Demonstration?
options: LPE elevates access from a low-privileged user to root/SYSTEM; Persistence documents how an adversary maintains long-term access (e.g., web shells, backdoor accounts, scheduled tasks)
LPE formats the target's disk; Persistence installs antivirus software
LPE scans external DNS servers; Persistence shuts down the target VM
Both terms refer strictly to running `nmap -sn` on an internal subnet
questions.answer: LPE elevates access from a low-privileged user to root/SYSTEM; Persistence documents how an adversary maintains long-term access (e.g., web shells, backdoor accounts, scheduled tasks)
questions.explanation: Post-exploitation validates how deeply an attacker could entrench themselves by escalating privileges locally and demonstrating persistence mechanisms.

questions.question: Which set of tools is specifically cited in the Week 10 lecture for automated Vulnerability Assessment scanning, and how frequently is VA typically run?
options: Nessus, Qualys, and OpenVAS; run continuously, weekly, or monthly
Ghidra, x64dbg, and IDA Pro; run once every ten years
Autopsy, FTK Imager, and Volatility; run only after a courtroom subpoena
Filebeat, Kafka, and Logstash; run strictly during software compilation
questions.answer: Nessus, Qualys, and OpenVAS; run continuously, weekly, or monthly
questions.explanation: Automated VA scanners (Nessus, Qualys, OpenVAS) run on a continuous, weekly, or monthly cadence, whereas Penetration Tests are typically conducted annually or after major infrastructure changes.

questions.question: In PTES Phase 6 (Reporting & Remediation Support), what distinguishes the Executive Summary from the Technical Findings section?
options: The Executive Summary translates risk, compliance impact, and security posture for leadership; Technical Findings provide reproduction steps, PoC code, affected assets, CVSS scores, and remediation steps
The Executive Summary lists every raw TCP packet; Technical Findings contain only budget spreadsheets
The Executive Summary is only for external hackers; Technical Findings are never shared with developers
Both sections contain only CVSS 0.0 Info findings
questions.answer: The Executive Summary translates risk, compliance impact, and security posture for leadership; Technical Findings provide reproduction steps, PoC code, affected assets, CVSS scores, and remediation steps
questions.explanation: Good PT reports serve both audiences: non-technical leadership (business risk and compliance) and technical engineers (reproduction steps, PoCs, CVSS, remediation).
